extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (Kantian aesthetics/teleology), advanced readers of metaphysics and philosophy of biology
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts methodological principles for judging natural purposiveness (teleology) as presented in Kant's Critique of Judgment: how to balance mechanical explanation and teleological (purpose-based) judgement, where teleology belongs in philosophy, and what heuristic constraints govern its use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teleology is a maxim of the reflective, not determinant Judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Teleology (the judgement according to purposes) is only a maxim of the reflective Judgement and is subjectively valid for us, not an objective (determinant) principle for the possibility of things themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat teleology as providing constitutive, objective explanations of natural production; it guides our judgement about nature but does not establish how natural productions come into being. It furnishes a regulative Idea rather than an a priori explanatory ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not eliminate mechanism; use mechanical explanation as far as possible
rubrics_metrics.description: It is infinitely important for Reason not to let slip the mechanism of nature in its products; explanations by mechanical causes must not be passed by because without them no insight into the nature of things can be attained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pursue mechanical explanations (the principle of the universal mechanism of matter) as far as probability and empirical investigation allow. Comparative anatomy and inquiry into physical laws are praiseworthy and necessary methods. However, recognize the human limits in fully accounting for organised beings mechanically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordinate the mechanical to the teleological when judging organised beings
rubrics_metrics.description: Although mechanical explanation should be pursued, for objects judged as natural purposes (organised beings) the judgement must finally subordinate mechanical grounds to a teleological principle because, by the constitution of our Understanding, designed causality is required for their possibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an object is indubitably an organised being, adopt as the basis an original organisation that employs mechanical means as instruments of a purposive cause. Practically: explain what you can mechanically, but ultimately judge organismic form as purposive and subordinate mechanical causes to that purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat teleology as a methodological/regulative discipline, not as part of Natural Science or Theology
rubrics_metrics.description: Teleology properly belongs neither to Natural Science (which requires determinant principles) nor to Theology as doctrine, but to Criticism—i.e., to the Methodology of the reflective Judgement that furnishes a way to judge nature according to final causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use teleology to guide how we systematise and describe nature (a guiding thread), and as heuristic for research; do not attempt to subsume teleology as a constitutive part of empirical natural science nor as doctrinal theology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanism and teleology are distinct explanatory methods and cannot be united as constitutive explanations for the same product
rubrics_metrics.description: One method of explanation (mechanical) excludes the other (teleological) as a constitutive, determinant principle for the same natural product; they do not coalesce as determinant grounds within empirical explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to derive a natural product from both principles as dogmatic explanatory grounds. If both seem to apply, recognize that their objective reconciliation would rest on a higher (supersensible) principle beyond empirical explanation; therefore keep the methods separate in determinant arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: When apparent contradiction arises between mechanisms and final causes, appeal to a supersensible common ground (heuristically, not explanatorily)
rubrics_metrics.description: The possibility that mechanism and teleology coexist objectively must be placed in a supersensible ground which we cannot determine positively; this explains why both observation of mechanical laws and teleological judgement can be warranted while their union cannot be fully explained empirically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the supersensible as a regulative hypothesis to account for the compatibility of both principles; do not treat it as an empirical explanatory tool. Acknowledge that any deeper reconciliation is beyond our determinative understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teleology is a heuristic for investigating particular laws of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Although teleological explanation does not render the origination of products any more comprehensible, it serves as a heuristic principle for discovering and investigating the particular laws of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use teleological concepts to guide empirical investigation (e.g., to hypothesize function, systematic relations, or comparative frameworks), but avoid substituting teleological posits for empirical, mechanical inquiry. Do not teleologise everything indiscriminately—proceed with caution and only where purposiveness appears undeniable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of purposiveness in organised beings (do not judge preservative parts as unpurposive)
rubrics_metrics.description: In an organised being the generation of its like is closely bound with the condition that nothing taken up into generative power belongs to the system except what is among its undeveloped original capacities; therefore one should not judge as unpurposive any part that contributes to the maintenance or propagation of the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the teleological principle conservatively: judge no component of an organism as merely accidental/unpurposive if it contributes to preservation or propagation. This principle legitimizes treating many features as purposive in systematic biological judgement, though it is ultimately a heuristic assumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Occasionalism in teleological methodology; favour hypotheses that preserve natural inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming Occasionalism (that the Supreme Cause creates each organised being immediately on each occasion) destroys natural inquiry and renders Reason useless in judging natural productions; better to adopt pre-established harmony models (preformation/epigenesis) if one must posit a metaphysical background.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject explanations that exempt nature from lawful study (occasional creation per instance). If a metaphysical account is invoked, prefer hypotheses that allow nature to operate lawfully (e.g., preformation/epigenesis variants) so that scientific investigation remains meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ comparative and historical (archaeological) methods to seek mechanical accounts where plausible
rubrics_metrics.description: It is permissible (and hopeful) for the 'archaeologist' of nature to seek, from surviving traces and comparative anatomy, whether a mechanical origin and common type can account for the variety of organised beings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empirical methods—comparative anatomy, tracing historical transformations, looking for common 'original type'—to test whether purposive forms can be partly or wholly accounted for by mechanical processes. But maintain the teleological regulative perspective when mechanical accounts remain inadequate.
